Sock hop
SOK hop
noun (Silent Generation slang)
American high-school word of the late 1940s and 1950s. Dances were held in school gymnasiums, and students were asked to take off their hard-soled shoes to protect the varnished floor, dancing in their socks — hence sock hop, with hop an older slang word for an informal dance. The records came from a turntable on the stage, and the dance became one of the fixed memories of 1950s teenage life.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A sock hop in 1955 was a Friday night in the gym: crepe-paper streamers, a record player on the stage, a chaperone by the punch bowl, and two hundred pairs of saddle shoes lined up by the door because the coach would not have them scuffing his floor. Girls in full skirts and boys in pressed slacks danced in their socks. For most of them it was clean, happy, and awkward. Scripture does not frown on that kind of joy. There is "a time to mourn, and a time to dance" (Ecc 3:4), and when the prodigal came home, his brother "heard musick and dancing" (Luk 15:25). The Psalmist could even say of God, "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing" (Psa 30:11). The shoes by the gym door bring another picture to mind. When Moses came near the burning bush, the Lord said, "put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground" (Exo 3:5). A sock hop was not holy ground, but the habit of taking care for the place you stand is a good one. Grandparents can teach the young that joy is a gift, that the dance floor has its proper limits, and that the deepest gladness is the gladness of the Father who runs to meet a returning son. Every lesser celebration points to that one.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (American high school, late 1940s–50s) for an informal dance held in the gym with shoes off to save the floor — a picture of the proper "time to dance" (Ecc 3:4) and of joy kept within bounds.

expand to see more

SOCK HOP, n. (Silent Generation slang, late 1940s–50s) An informal school dance, usually in a gymnasium, where students danced in their socks to protect the floor. "Are you going to the sock hop after the game Friday?"

Webster (1828) — SOCK, noun [Latin soccus; ] 1. The shoe of the ancient actors of comedy. Hence the word is used for comedy, and opposed to buskin or tragedy. 2. A garment for the foot, like the foot of a stocking.

Decode for families: shoes off for the floor’s sake; joy with limits for the soul’s sake.

Key Scripture

Ecc 3:4 — "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;"

Luk 15:25 — "Now his elder son was in the field: and as he came and drew nigh to the house, he heard musick and dancing."

Psa 30:11 — "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness;"

Exo 3:5 — "And he said, Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground."

Modern Corruption

A wholesome word for clean, chaperoned fun; the only caution is the old one that every dance floor needs boundaries of modesty and purity.

expand to see more

There is very little to correct in sock hop. Chaperoned school dances with punch and records were among the most innocent amusements of any generation, and Scripture plainly allows for joy and dancing (Ecc 3:4).

The caution is perennial rather than particular. As the music changed later in the decade, some dances grew less modest, and a few young people slipped out to the parking lot. The old wisdom holds: rejoice in the gift, keep the bounds of purity, and let every celebration remain one a grandparent could watch without blushing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin soccus (light shoe) → Old English socc → sock + slang hop (informal dance) → sock hop (late 1940s–50s school gym dance).

expand to see more

Latin soccus — a light, low shoe worn by comic actors

Old English socc — a light slipper; later a short stocking

18th c. slang hop — an informal dance

Late 1940s–50s: sock hop, the shoeless dance in the school gym

Usage

""Your grandmother and I met at a sock hop in 1954. I stepped on her toes all night — at least I was in my socks.""

"Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing (Psa 30:11)."

"Let them praise his name in the dance (Psa 149:3)."
